original_question: Do both pure red cell aplasia (PRCA) and Diamond-Blackfan anemia (DBA) lead to low red blood cell counts without significantly affecting white blood cells?

final_qi.question: Do both pure red cell aplasia (PRCA) and Diamond-Blackfan anemia (DBA) lead to low red blood cell counts?
final_qi.long_answer:
Both conditions are characterized by a marked reduction in erythroid precursors in the bone marrow, resulting in decreased production of mature red blood cells. 

• Pure red cell aplasia (PRCA) — whether acquired (e.g., autoimmune, parvovirus B19–related, drug-induced) or congenital — produces a profound, often normocytic, anemia with very low reticulocyte counts while leaving white blood cell and platelet production largely intact. The defining feature is a markedly reduced red blood cell (RBC) mass. 

• Diamond-Blackfan anemia (DBA) is an inherited ribosomopathy in which mutations in ribosomal protein genes impair erythroid progenitor survival and proliferation. Affected infants and children develop macrocytic anemia with severely depressed reticulocyte and RBC counts, again with relatively preserved non-erythroid lineages. 

Because the central pathophysiology of both PRCA and DBA is selective failure of erythroid production, each disorder leads to abnormally low circulating red blood cell counts (clinical anemia). Therefore, the statement is correct.

final_qi.question: Do both pure red cell aplasia (PRCA) and Diamond-Blackfan anemia (DBA) significantly affect white blood cell counts?
final_qi.long_answer: Both pure red cell aplasia (PRCA) and Diamond-Blackfan anemia (DBA) are characterized by an isolated failure of the erythroid (red-cell) lineage. In classic acquired PRCA, leukocyte and platelet production in the bone marrow remain normal, so white blood cell (WBC) counts are typically within the normal range. Likewise, DBA—often described as a congenital form of pure red cell aplasia—shows profound anemia and reticulocytopenia, but neutrophil and platelet counts are generally preserved. Although mild neutropenia can occasionally be seen in DBA, a significant or characteristic depression of WBC counts is not part of the defining clinical picture for either disorder. Therefore, it is incorrect to state that both conditions significantly affect white blood cell counts.
